title: Lossy detection and adaptive fallbacks for OpenAI Responses compatibility
creator: Liam Chen
description:
Problem summary: When exposing an OpenAI Responses compatibility surface we observe subtle lossy transformations between the source OpenAI event model and Redwood's runtime event/stream model. Lossy cases manifest as: dropped function-call args in chunked streams, mis-ordered streaming events for structured output markers, missing tool-call metadata (eg. tool invocation_id) after runtime batching, and truncated JSON-in-structured-output when token boundary splits occur. These cases cause downstream SDKs and customer integrations to either error or silently produce incorrect behavior.

Objective: Implement runtime heuristics and a light-weight compatibility layer that (1) detects likely lossy translation at request- and token-level, (2) applies adaptive fallbacks to preserve semantics (reconstruction, metadata amplification, graceful fallback to blocking call), and (3) surfaces clear telemetry and developer-facing hints for remediation. The goal is to reduce customer-visible failures for OpenAI Responses-style integrations by 90% for common patterns without impacting latency SLOs for non-compat traffic.
technical_design:
Design overview: add a compat detector that attaches a small per-request 'compat-context' during routing when the request declares 'openai_responses' or when the SDK compatibility header is present. Detector heuristics: 1) streaming-event-sequence validation: ensure required event order (start -> token/chunk -> function_call_start -> function_call_args -> function_call_end -> end). If gaps or out-of-order fragments are detected, increment compat_loss counters and trigger reconstruction flow. 2) chunk-boundary JSON sanity: attempt to re-parse incremental structured-output buffers; if partial parse fails after N tokens, buffer up to M tokens and attempt reconstitution before emitting to client. 3) metadata persistence checks: verify tool-call metadata (invocation_id, tool_name, call_signature) survives batching/sharing across worker boundaries — if missing, synthesize from cached preflight headers. 4) idempotency & dedupe: if duplicate events appear (due to retries), dedupe based on event-hash and timestamp window.

Adaptive fallbacks: A) Inline reconstruction: for mild cases, runtime combines buffered chunks and emits a reconstituted structured object with a compat_meta hint. B) Blocking escalation: if reconstruction cannot be guaranteed within latency budget, automatically route that single request to a blocking call path (no streaming) to preserve correctness. C) Tool-call signature fallback: if function-call args are incomplete, invoke the configured tool-call shim to re-request the missing payload from the model (a short follow-up prompt) and attach the recovered args as a 'compat_fix' envelope.

Implementation notes: implement detector as a middleware in the stream-router; add a lightweight in-memory per-request buffer with size cap (default 128KB). Expose runtime flags: COMPAT_BUFFER_SIZE, COMPAT_BLOCKING_TIMEOUT_MS. Instrumentation: counters for compat_loss_detected, compat_reconstructions, compat_block_escalations, compat_fix_success_rate. Log structured events to kinesis/compat-events topic with sampling for postmortem.

Backward compatibility: default behavior is opt-in via header X-Redwood-Compat: openai-responses; we will enable for a small canary org list. Non-compat traffic unaffected.
acceptance_criteria:
1) Detector increments compat_loss_detected and emits a kinesis event when a lossy pattern is detected.
2) For synthetic test cases (see test_plan), 90% of truncated JSON structured outputs are reconstructed correctly by the inline reconstruction flow.
3) Blocking escalation path preserves full original model response for high-loss cases and returns a compat_meta flag set to 'blocking_escalation'.
4) Metrics emitted to console show compat_reconstructions and compat_fix_success_rate; alerts fire if compat_loss_detected rate > 0.5% for canary orgs.
5) End-to-end SDK integration tests pass (tool-calling + streaming + structured output) with no regressions for non-compat traffic.
test_plan:
- Unit tests for event-sequence validation (ordered/out-of-order/missing)
- Fuzz tests that split JSON objects at random token boundaries and assert reconstruction correctness within buffer size limits
- Integration test harness that replays recorded OpenAI Responses streams with known problematic sequences (from ENG-21456 incident logs) and asserts compat_fix paths execute
- Load test: run canary org traffic with compat layer enabled at 5% production traffic to check latency P95 impact (target < +10ms)
- Canary rollout observations: monitor compat_loss_detected, compat_block_escalations, request latency buckets, and error rates.
rollout_plan: 1) Merge behind feature flag and enable for internal org + test tenants. 2) Stage canary: enable for 5% of traffic for a curated set of customers that have opted-in. 3) Monitor for 72 hours; if compat_block_escalations spike above threshold, revert or adjust buffer/timeouts. 4) Gradually increase to 25% then 100% for canary cohort after 2 weeks and sign-off from SRE and Runtime PM. 5) Post-rollout: publish compatibility notes to SDKs with migration hints and new header options.
risks_and_mitigation:
- Risk: Buffering and reconstruction could increase P95 latency. Mitigation: strict caps and fallback to blocking escalation to bound tail.
- Risk: False positives in detector cause unnecessary escalations. Mitigation: conservative default thresholds and sampling for analysis before widening.
- Risk: Synthesized metadata could be incorrect for exotic tool-call flows. Mitigation: prefer to escalate to blocking path for higher-risk tool contracts and log occurrences for manual review.
- Risk: Increased operational costs for extra writes to compat-events stream. Mitigation: sample events and use tiered retention.
